description:
We are six Computer Engineering students from Rafaela, Argentina, united by our passion for technology, innovation, and space exploration.

For the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, we are developing a solution that transforms complex lunar data into actionable insights to help identify and evaluate potential landing sites.

Combining software engineering, data analysis, and creativity, we aim to contribute to safer and smarter lunar exploration. Six minds, one mission: helping humanity take its next steps on the Moon.
summary: If you have ever camped, you already know the problem: you need sun to charge your gear and signal to tell someone you are fine. A Moon lander needs exactly the same, and the wrong landing date can cost it either one. Lunar Landing Site Navigator answers "if I land here on this date, will I have Sun and a direct link to Earth?" on one screen. Pick one of 14 landing sites (Apollo, CLPS, Chang'e, Chandrayaan, SLIM), type any coordinates or click a point on the polar map, and choose a date. The app draws the local sky with the Sun and Earth over the site's real LOLA terrain horizon, shows the hours of sunlight and Earth visibility for the next seven days, and counts down to the next sunset or Earthset. Two or three site-date scenarios can be compared side by side. Positions come from NASA/JPL Horizons and the terrain from NASA LRO/LOLA; our code computes visibility. Automated tests check our values against 432 saved Horizons answers (largest difference 0.0005°), and our sunlight percentages match LOLA's independent illumination maps. The data already exists in NASA's tools, but they are built for specialists. We made it fast for mission planners, educators and the public. Try it: https://vizcachasfueradeorbita.vercel.app/?lang=en
details:
The problem. Near the lunar south pole, the Sun skims the horizon, while Earth slowly moves up and down across it because of lunar libration. A small change in location or time can mean the difference between continuous sunlight and prolonged darkness, or between a direct communication link and an outage.

NASA and JPL tools such as Horizons, LROC Quickmap and Moon Trek provide the data to study these conditions. But answering a practical mission question ("Will this site have sunlight and direct communication with Earth on a given date?") requires combining several datasets, understanding lunar geometry, and accounting for local terrain obstructions. We tested these tools against that question, and none gave the complete answer in a single workflow.

What it does.

- Choosing where to land: three ways, all leading to the same result screen. Pick one of 14 mission sites (Apollo, CLPS, Chang'e, Chandrayaan, SLIM), each with a verified source for its coordinates; type any latitude and longitude; or click a point on a 2D map of the lunar polar regions.

- Sky view: a 3D sky with the Sun and Earth as discs over the site's horizon, plus a compass and an elevation ruler. The Sun's elevation is the most prominent number, because it drives solar power. The app tells "below the horizon" apart from "hidden by terrain".

- Time: a time player, a 7-day timeline of when each body is above the horizon, and a live countdown to the next sunset, sunrise, Earthset or Earthrise.

- Historic mission mode: see the sky on the landing day of each mission.

- Comparison: two or three site-date scenarios side by side, with Sun hours and Earth hours over seven days. The app does not declare a winner: which metric matters depends on the mission, so it marks the leader of each one and the user decides.

- Validation panel: our values next to JPL Horizons reference values, with the difference.

- Plain language, mobile layout, and four interface languages (English, Spanish, Hindi, Simplified Chinese).

How it works. A Python pipeline queries the JPL Horizons API for the topocentric azimuth and elevation of the Sun and Earth at each site, one sample per hour (DE441 ephemeris, apparent positions, no atmosphere), and stores them as JSON. The horizon is a 360-direction profile out to 20 km, built from LRO/LOLA elevation data from NASA Moon Trek: the 30 m South Pole model for IM-1 and IM-2, and the 128 ppd global model for the other 12 sites. The web app (JavaScript, Vite, three.js) reads these precomputed files, so the 14 mission sites need no backend. For a free point, a small FastAPI service queries Horizons live and computes the LOLA horizon on the fly; above 85° N there is no map, so the horizon is flat and the app says so. A body counts as visible when the upper edge of its disc is above the horizon. Python and the web app exchange data only through JSON files that follow a written data contract and JSON Schema.

What is new / impact. Real terrain changes the answer, in both directions. Compared with a smooth Moon, LOLA terrain removes about 11% of the Sun hours at Intuitive Machines 2 and about 25% at Odysseus (IM-1) over the 426 days in our data, while at IM-2 it adds about 18% more Earth hours, because parts of its horizon lie below the smooth-Moon horizon. A launch delay changes the picture too: landing at IM-2 on 8 November 2026 gives 0 Sun hours in the following seven days, while landing on 15 November 2026 gives 166. The same screen serves mission planners comparing options, teachers, and anyone curious about why the Moon is hard.

How we checked it (validity). A plausible-looking but wrong angle is the worst failure, so we verified the conventions (azimuth from north, east-positive longitude, UTC) against Horizons before generating any site. Automated tests compare our values with saved Horizons responses, and the in-app validation panel shows them side by side: the largest difference is 0.0005° across 432 values, against a 0.1° tolerance. As an independent check of the terrain, our sunlight percentages match LOLA's average-illumination maps (Mazarico et al. 2011): IM-2 45.9% (ours) vs 45.0-46.8% (LOLA); IM-1 37.8% vs 35.6-41.1%; Chandrayaan-3 47.2% vs 48.3%. About 550 automated tests cover the data and the app. Limits we state openly: twelve sites use the 237 m global DEM and terrain is considered out to 20 km; sunset and sunrise times are estimated by interpolating hourly samples; and the ground texture and stars in the sky view are decorative.

What comes next. Finer terrain for more sites, a best-landing-window finder, and power and communication budgets for specific landers
